purpose: Sumatriptan is used to treat migraine headaches, with or without aura (visual disturbances like flashing lights). It can also treat cluster headaches. It is not used to prevent migraines — only to stop one that has already started.
how_it_works: When a migraine starts, certain blood vessels in your brain swell up and cause pain. Sumatriptan works by attaching to receptors in those blood vessels and causing them to narrow back down to normal size. It also helps block pain signals in the brain, which helps relieve the headache, nausea, and light sensitivity that come with migraines.
common_side_effects: You might feel a warm or tingling sensation, flushing, dizziness, or drowsiness after taking it. Some people feel tightness or pressure in the chest, neck, or jaw — this is usually harmless but let your doctor know if it happens. Nausea and a feeling of heaviness in the arms or legs can also occur.
warnings: Do not use sumatriptan if you have heart disease, a history of stroke, uncontrolled high blood pressure, or certain types of migraines (hemiplegic or basilar migraines). Do not take it within 24 hours of other triptan medications or ergotamine-type drugs. Overusing this medication (more than 10 days per month) can actually cause more frequent headaches over time, called medication overuse headache. Always tell your doctor about all medications you take, especially antidepressants, as serious interactions can occur.
typical_dosing: For tablets, the usual starting dose is 25 mg to 100 mg taken at the first sign of a migraine. If the headache comes back or only partially improves, you can take a second dose at least 2 hours later. Do not take more than 200 mg in one day. For the nasal spray or injection, dosing is different, so always follow your doctor or pharmacist's specific instructions for your form of the medication.
